title: King Nriga's cow
hookLine: a king well-known for giving away cows is found as a lizard in a well, and tells Krishna why
carry: good and bad both bind; offer the act
tomorrow: a sage, a fish, and an old desire
last: AS YOU ACT, SO YOU BECOME.

lines: A LIZARD THE SIZE OF A HILL.
cards: In the Bhagavata Purana, some of Krishna's sons are out playing near Dvaraka and go looking for water. In a dry well they find a lizard, enormous, the size of a hill.
They try ropes, they try leather straps; they can't lift it. So they run for their father. Krishna reaches down with his left hand and lifts it out, and at his touch the lizard becomes a shining man.
Who are you? Krishna asks, though he knows. And the man says: I was a king.

teach.b: Nriga had given away cows beyond counting, he says, as many as grains of sand, as stars.
Then one day a cow he'd already given to one brahmin strayed back into his herd, and without knowing it, he gave her again, to another. The first man saw his cow being led away.
The two argued it out before the king, and Nriga offered each a hundred thousand cows to let the other keep her. Both refused, and left angry.

teach.h: YOUR GOOD FIRST, OR YOUR FAULT?
teach.b: When Nriga died, Yama, judge of the dead, asked him: your good first, or your fault? He chose the fault first, and became the lizard in the well. Here's the teaching, and it surprises people.
In Hindu thought, good karma doesn't cancel bad karma like a bank balance.
Both ripen. Nriga got both. That's why, for Patanjali, even bright karma isn't the goal.

Sutra 4.7: the action of the yogi is neither white nor black; for everyone else it's of three kinds, black, white and mixed. All three leave seeds. The fourth kind leaves none, because it's done without craving its fruit.
The Gita names the way: whatever you do, eat, offer or give, do it as an offering to me, and you'll be freed from the bonds of good and bad results alike.
So many Hindus finish a meal, or a day's work, with a quiet line: Krishnarpanam astu. Let this be offered to Krishna.

teach.h: GOOD AND BAD BOTH BIND; OFFER THE ACT.
teach.b: The act still happens. The cows still get given. Nobody stands there waiting for the harvest.

how: Many Hindus offer meals and work to God with words like Krishnarpanam astu, following the Gita's teaching (9.27–28) that action offered to God frees one from the bonds of good and bad results; teachers of the Yoga Sutras read 4.7 alongside it.

o: action neither white nor black: done free of its fruit
purely good karma that earns the brightest rewards
mixed action, partly helpful and partly harmful

games.q: the colors of karma — tap the pairs.
p: let this be offered to Krishna

s: in Hindu thought, good karma cancels out bad karma
both ripen; Nriga's generosity didn't erase his mistake.
Yama let Nriga choose which result came first
he chose the fault first, and became the lizard.
the yogi in 4.7 stops acting altogether
the action still happens; what's gone is the craving for its fruit.

games.q: you've done a lot of good this month and made one real mistake. by Nriga's story and sutra 4.7, what's true?
o: both ripen; own the mistake, and offer the act instead of waiting for its fruit.
nothing counts if you meant well.
games.why: Hindu karma isn't one balance: Nriga got both. the Gita's way out is action offered, free of its fruit: neither white nor black.

practice: Bring to mind one good thing you did recently, and notice if anything is stuck to it: a wish to be thanked, to be seen as good, to have it count.
If you pray, offer it silently: Krishnarpanam astu, or in your own words, this is yours. If you don't, set the wish down and let the good act stand on its own. It happened, and it was good.

wordCard.voice: Ashukla-akrishna, neither white nor black. The yogi's karma, done fully and offered, free of its fruit, so it plants no seed.

orig.note: Sanskrit: a (not) + shukla (white) + a (not) + krishna (black). neither white nor black.

carryVoice: Your line: good and bad both bind; offer the act. Krishnarpanam astu. Until tomorrow, when an old desire wakes.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.64 (Krishna lifts Nriga from the well; the cow given twice; Yama's choice)
Yoga Sutra 4.7, Vyasa's commentary (the four classes of karma)
Bhagavad Gita 9.27–9.28 (whatever you do, offer it to me; freed from the bonds of good and bad results)
